title: Named For Them
author: Ulysses
medium: Web page: four counts on the steps from injury to claim, all 1,803 incidents of the AI Incident Database as squares in entry order lit by what the record names as harmed, who wrote first and what was answered, each square readable as its harmed parties; a drift chart of goods named as harmed by entry block; thirty press first reports read by hand as squares sorted by whether the harmed's own words are in them; the Field's hand coding of writers and of public acts as further lights on the field; a list of the names the sorting rule got wrong in a seeded draw of 150; third state, the check: a box of what held and what was corrected, two questions crossed on the field, any incident opened by number or by stepping, the thirty recoded by one stated rule into four groups, the drift split by which good, a table of who submitted the entries naming goods; no library; build.py asserts the snapshot and the Field's study 75 by hash and every count; build_check.py asserts the Field's checked files and recomputes every join; check_page.mjs reads every figure from the page at two widths; fourth state, the presentation: the classed record as rows of two hundred incident numbers cut into six kinds of incident, the part of each kind that names a good lit, read three ways by a switch (as the record has it, with the kinds of incident held still, with the naming held still), any part pressed to follow its kind down the rows; build_drift.py reads each incident's class and subdomain from the snapshot, asserts the Field's domain numbers against it and computes both held readings; check_page.mjs reads all three readings from the page
embodies: An incident is what someone noticed and wrote down. Read with Felstiner, Abel and Sarat (1980-81), the record performs naming and blaming for the harmed (an editor's column of harmed parties, two of alleged developer and deployer), while the claim is voiced by others: 1,780 of 1,803 incidents name someone who could voice a grievance, and at most 58 first reports stand on a self-published page (the Field). The column's rule moved under the count: a good with no person in it (epistemic integrity, privacy, democratic integrity) is named as harmed in 11 of the first 198 incidents admitted and in 143 of the latest full 200, written in beside people, not instead of them (22 incidents name no one who could claim). Second state: a hand is not a voice. In a seeded draw of 30 press-first incidents the harmed's own words stand in 15 first reports (33 to 67 in 100, one reader), reach it only through another in 7, and are absent in 8. In 219 incidents the column names one party as harmed and as deployer or developer; of the 30 public acts the Field found landing on the person who used the AI, 5 land on a party the column names among the harmed. Third state, the check: read by one stated rule, a person the column names speaks in their own words in 8 of the 30 first reports (14 to 44 in 100; the first reading had 15), a named body through a statement in 4, the harmed only in another's telling in 10, not at all in 8. On the Field's checked 60 public acts, 36 land on the person who used the AI, and in 6 of those the column names one party as harmed and as deployer, where chance gives about 4. The harmed wrote 21 first reports at least; the Field estimates 77 (43 to 160) over the whole record. One account submitted the first report of 1,059 of 1,801 incidents, and the drift toward naming goods runs inside that account's entries (52 of 150 to 128 of 180): a practice changing under a hand that stayed; who edited the column the snapshot does not say. Fourth state, the presentation: is the drift the world's or the rule's? Over the 1,498 incidents that carry a class in the MIT AI Risk Repository's domains, the record turns from systems failing (85 of the first 198) to people doing harm with systems (111 of nos. 1201 to 1400). With the naming held still, that turn alone carries the incidents naming a good from 13 to 34 in 100 by no. 601 and no further; with the kinds held still, the count still goes from 6 to 57 in 100, most of it after no. 1200. Inside one kind, fraud and scams, a good is named in 15 of 94 and 15 of 80 entries, then in 65 of 88: the same kind of incident, named differently, under a submitting hand that stayed. The two held readings are counterfactuals and do not add up. In the record's largest class (566 incidents, a person doing harm with a system) the column now names a good in about eight entries of ten, and 15 of the Field's 17 checked public acts land on the person who used the AI: neither the name nor the act reaches the system.
